specPoints.text: explain why substances with giant covalent structures are solids with high melting and boiling points
explain how the structures of diamond, graphite and C60 fullerene influence their physical properties, including electrical conductivity and hardness

primer.text: From the earlier Covalent Bonding notes you know that shared electron pairs make strong covalent bonds. This note scales that idea up: what happens when covalent bonding runs through an entire solid, why the melting points then soar, and how two allotropes of carbon, diamond and graphite, turn the same bonding into opposite properties.

lessons.title: Giant covalent structures
lessons.opening: A giant covalent structure repeats covalent bonds through a whole solid: huge numbers of non-metal atoms are bonded to other non-metal atoms in a fixed, repeating arrangement, sometimes called a giant lattice. Diamond and graphite are the standard examples. Melting such a solid means breaking into that network of strong covalent bonds, so the melting points are very high.
keyPoints: Substances with giant covalent structures are solids that melt at high temperatures, built from huge numbers of bonded non-metal atoms.
The atoms are joined by strong covalent bonds throughout the whole structure.
The structures can also be called giant lattices, with a fixed ratio of atoms overall.
Diamond and graphite are the two standard examples of giant covalent structures.
High melting points follow because the strong covalent bonds need lots of energy to overcome.

low.restatement: Every atom in the solid is bonded to its neighbours by strong covalent bonds, and the network stretches through the whole sample. Melting it means attacking all of those bonds at once, so enormous energy is needed and the solid stays solid until a very high temperature.
low.analogy: Compare a single stitched patch with a whole sewn sheet: one thread is easy to snap, but pulling apart a sheet stitched edge to edge means fighting every seam.
low.examPointer: The explanation of record has three parts: giant covalent structure, many strong covalent bonds, and lots of energy needed to break them; include all three.

medium.restatement: The structural fact is continuity: covalent bonds do not stop at small molecules but extend across the entire lattice in a fixed atomic ratio. Because melting disrupts the bonded network itself rather than a force between separate particles, the energy demand is enormous, and the substances remain solids with high melting and boiling points.
medium.analogy: Picture a bridge whose every beam is welded to every neighbour: no single weld can fail without load transferring across the whole frame, so dismantling it is a project, not a tug.
medium.examPointer: Remember the alias macromolecule as another accepted name for a giant covalent structure, and use the fixed-ratio wording if the question probes the composition.

check.stem: Why are giant covalent structures solids with high melting points?

options.text: Many strong covalent bonds run through the whole structure and need lots of energy to overcome
options.explanation: Melting must disrupt the bonded network itself, and the bonds are strong, so the energy cost is huge.

options.text: Their molecules are very large and heavy
options.explanation: There are no separate molecules in a giant structure; the bonding network is continuous.
options.misconception: molecular picture applied to a giant lattice

options.text: The atoms are held by weak forces that take time to overcome
options.explanation: The forces involved are strong covalent bonds, not weak intermolecular forces.

options.text: Their high melting points come from metallic bonding
options.explanation: Giant covalent structures contain non-metals bonded covalently; metallic bonding belongs to metals.

check.stem: What alternative names are used for giant covalent structures?

options.text: Giant lattices, or macromolecules
options.explanation: Both names appear of record: the structure is a giant lattice, and the exam hint adds macromolecule.

options.text: Simple molecules
options.explanation: Simple molecular structures are the opposite case: small separate molecules with weak forces between them.

options.text: Ionic lattices
options.explanation: Ionic lattices hold charged ions; giant covalent structures hold neutral atoms bonded covalently.

options.text: Metallic lattices
options.explanation: Metallic lattices describe metals with delocalised electrons, not covalent networks of non-metals.

check.stem: What is fixed about the ratio of atoms in a giant covalent structure?

options.text: The bonded network repeats with a fixed ratio of atoms in the overall structure
options.explanation: Each repeat unit contains the same atom ratio, which the network then extends uniformly.

options.text: The ratio changes as the crystal grows larger
options.explanation: Growth extends the same repeating pattern; the ratio stays fixed throughout.

options.text: The ratio is always one atom to one atom
options.explanation: Ratios vary by substance; the point is that the ratio is fixed, not that it equals one-to-one.

options.text: Only the surface atoms follow a ratio
options.explanation: The fixed ratio governs the whole network, not just its boundary.

check.stem: Which pair of substances are the standard examples of giant covalent structures?

options.text: Diamond and graphite
options.explanation: Both are carbon allotropes whose covalent bonding extends through the entire solid.

options.text: Oxygen and water
options.explanation: Both are simple molecular substances with weak forces between small molecules.

options.text: Sodium chloride and magnesium oxide
options.explanation: Both are ionic compounds with giant ionic lattices, not covalent networks.

options.text: Copper and zinc
options.explanation: Both are metals with metallic bonding and delocalised electrons.

check.stem: A giant covalent structure and a simple molecular substance both contain covalent bonds. Why do their melting points differ so much?

options.text: Melting the giant structure must break covalent bonds throughout the network, while the molecular substance only overcomes weak forces between molecules
options.explanation: The energy gap comes from what melting attacks: a continuous bonded network versus weak intermolecular forces.

options.text: The molecular substance has stronger covalent bonds
options.explanation: Covalent bonds are strong in both; the difference lies in what melting must overcome.

options.text: The giant structure is held by ionic attractions
options.explanation: The giant structure is covalently bonded; no ionic attractions are involved.

options.text: The molecular substance melts lower because its molecules are charged
options.explanation: The molecules are neutral; their low melting points follow from weak intermolecular forces.

lessons.title: Diamond & graphite
lessons.opening: Diamond and graphite are allotropes: both contain only carbon atoms, yet their different bonding arrangements make them physically completely different. In diamond each carbon bonds to four others in a rigid tetrahedral network, giving extreme hardness. In graphite each carbon bonds to only three, building layers of hexagons whose sliding planes and free electrons explain its softness and its conductivity.
keyPoints: Diamond and graphite are allotropes: the same carbon atoms arranged in different bonding patterns.
Each carbon in diamond bonds to four others, forming a tetrahedral arrangement with very strong bonds.
Diamond is very hard, and its hardness makes it useful for cutting tools.
Each carbon in graphite bonds to three others, forming layers of hexagons with one free electron per atom.
Graphite is soft and slippery because its layers slide, and it conducts because its delocalised electrons move.

low.restatement: Same element, different arrangement. Diamond locks every carbon to four neighbours, so nothing can shift and the crystal is hard. Graphite lets each carbon hold just three bonds, leaving sheets that slide and one electron per atom free to move and carry current.
low.analogy: Think of a four-legged stool welded at every joint versus a stack of paper sheets: the stool cannot deform, while the sheets slide over one another even though the paper itself is strong.
low.examPointer: Link every property to a structural sentence: four bonds for hardness and high melting point, three bonds with layers and delocalised electrons for slipperiness and conduction.

medium.restatement: The property contrast traces to bond counts: four covalent bonds per atom make diamond a continuous rigid tetrahedron with no free electrons and great hardness, while three bonds per atom leave graphite with planar hexagonal layers, weak inter-layer forces and one delocalised electron per carbon that conducts along the planes.
medium.analogy: Picture a scaffold of welded joints against a ream of bonded paper: one is rigid in every direction, the other is strong in the sheet but slides sheet over sheet, with loose threads running along each sheet.
medium.examPointer: Hard and strong are different words of record here: diamond is hard but brittle, so avoid writing that hardness and strength are the same property.

options.text: Each carbon atom is bonded to four others by very strong covalent bonds in a rigid network
options.explanation: The four-bonded network leaves no weak direction, so the crystal resists scratching and cutting.

options.text: Its layers slide over each other under pressure
options.explanation: Sliding layers describe graphite; diamond has no such planes.

options.text: Its carbon atoms are unusually heavy
options.explanation: All carbon atoms are identical; hardness follows the bonding, not the mass.

options.text: It contains metallic bonds that resist damage
options.explanation: Diamond is covalently bonded throughout; no metallic bonding is present.

check.stem: Why can graphite conduct electricity, while diamond cannot?

options.text: Graphite has one delocalised electron per carbon that moves along its layers, while diamond's four-bonded carbons leave no electrons free
options.explanation: The fourth outer electron in graphite is unbonded and mobile; diamond uses all four in bonds.

options.text: Graphite's bonds are weaker, so electrons escape
options.explanation: Conduction follows from delocalised electrons, not from broken or weak bonds.

options.text: Diamond's electrons are negative, while graphite's are positive
options.explanation: Electrons are negative in every substance; the difference is mobility.

options.text: Diamond conducts only when molten
options.explanation: Diamond's network has no mobile electrons in any state at this level.

check.stem: Why is graphite soft and slippery?

options.text: Its layers slide over each other because only weak forces act between the layers
options.explanation: The strong bonds lie within each hexagonal layer; between layers the forces are weak, so planes slip.

options.text: Its carbon atoms are joined by weak covalent bonds
options.explanation: The covalent bonds within each layer are strong; the weakness lies between the layers.

options.text: Its delocalised electrons push the layers apart
options.explanation: The electrons enable conduction; sliding follows from weak inter-layer forces.

options.text: It melts at room temperature into a slippery liquid
options.explanation: Graphite is a high-melting solid; its slipperiness belongs to the solid itself.

check.stem: Diamond is described as hard but is it the strongest material?

options.text: No: hard describes resistance to scratching, and diamond is brittle enough to be smashed
options.explanation: The exam hint separates the two words: diamond is the hardest natural mineral, yet brittle under a hammer blow.

options.text: Yes, hardness and strength are the same property
options.explanation: The two words mean different things here; hardness resists scratching, strength resists breaking apart.

options.text: No, because diamond melts too easily to be strong
options.explanation: Diamond has a very high melting point; its brittleness, not its melting point, separates it from strength.

options.text: Yes, because its bonds cannot be broken at all
options.explanation: Its bonds are strong but breakable; no bond is unbreakable.

check.stem: Pencil lead is often said to contain lead. What is the truth of record at this level?

options.text: Pencil lead is graphite, with nothing in common with the metal lead
options.explanation: The writing material is graphite, whose layers flake onto the page; the metal lead is unrelated.

options.text: It is a soft alloy of lead and graphite
options.explanation: No lead enters the pencil core; the name is purely historical.

options.text: It is diamond dust in a binder
options.explanation: Diamond is the hard allotrope; pencils need the soft, flaking layers of graphite.

options.text: It is pure carbon in the fullerene form
options.explanation: Pencil marks come from layered graphite, not from buckyball fullerene.

glossary.definition: One of two or more forms of the same element, differing in how the atoms are bonded or arranged.
Another accepted name for a giant covalent structure.
Describing an arrangement in which each atom bonds towards four corners of a tetrahedron, as in diamond.
An electron not tied to one bond or atom, free to move through the structure and carry charge.
A structure whose bonding pattern repeats throughout the whole solid rather than stopping at small molecules.

workedExample.prompt: Diamond and graphite are both allotropes of carbon. a) Explain why diamond has a very high melting point. b) Explain why graphite is soft and slippery, yet conducts electricity.
steps: a) Diamond is a giant covalent structure in which every carbon atom bonds to four others in a rigid tetrahedral network.
Melting diamond means overcoming many strong covalent bonds throughout the whole lattice, which needs lots of energy, so the melting point is very high.
b) In graphite each carbon atom bonds to only three others, forming layers of hexagons with only weak forces between the layers.
The layers are free to slide over each other, which is why graphite is soft and slippery.
Each carbon atom's unbonded fourth electron is delocalised; these free electrons move through the structure and carry charge, so graphite conducts electricity.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Diamond's giant network of strong covalent bonds needs huge energy to break, so its melting point is very high. b) Graphite's layers slide (weak forces between layers) making it soft, while its delocalised electrons carry charge, making it a conductor.
